items.title: Estimating Cooling Rates of a Liquid from a Table
items.stem:
No calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Using the data at t = 3 and t = 7, estimate T′(5). Show the computation that leads to your answer and indicate units of measure.

(b) Using the two times in the table closest to t = 8.5, estimate T′(8.5). Show the computation that leads to your answer.

(c) Using the two greatest times in the table, estimate T′(12). Explain why your difference quotient cannot use a time later than t = 12.

(d) Based on your estimates from parts (a) and (c), is the temperature of the liquid decreasing faster at t = 5 or at t = 12? Justify your answer.
items.stimulus:
A cup of hot liquid is left on a counter to cool. Its temperature, in degrees Celsius (°C), is modeled by a differentiable function T of time t, in minutes, for 0 ≤ t ≤ 12. Selected values of T(t) are given in the table below.

t (minutes): 0 | 3 | 5 | 7 | 10 | 12
T(t) (°C): 90 | 78 | 71 | 65 | 57 | 53

Answer all parts of the following question. Show the computations that lead to your answers.
items.answer:
(a) T′(5) ≈ (T(7) − T(3))/(7 − 3) = (65 − 78)/4 = −13/4 = −3.25 °C per minute.

(b) The table times closest to 8.5 are t = 7 and t = 10.
T′(8.5) ≈ (T(10) − T(7))/(10 − 7) = (57 − 65)/3 = −8/3 ≈ −2.667 °C per minute.

(c) T′(12) ≈ (T(12) − T(10))/(12 − 10) = (53 − 57)/2 = −2 °C per minute.
The function is only defined, and data are only given, for 0 ≤ t ≤ 12, so there are no values after t = 12; the difference quotient must use an earlier time such as t = 10.

(d) The temperature is decreasing faster at t = 5. Both estimated rates are negative, and the magnitude of the estimate at t = 5 is 3.25 °C per minute, which is greater than the magnitude 2 °C per minute at t = 12 (equivalently −3.25 < −2).

criteria.text: Sets up the difference quotient (T(7) − T(3))/(7 − 3) = (65 − 78)/4.
criteria.evidence: Response shows a difference quotient using the table values at t = 3 and t = 7, with the change in temperature divided by the change in time.
criteria.fix: Divide the change in T by the change in t for the two given table times; write the quotient with both values before simplifying.

criteria.text: Obtains T′(5) ≈ −3.25 °C per minute, with correct units.
criteria.evidence: Response states the estimate −3.25 (or −13/4) together with the units degrees Celsius per minute.
criteria.fix: Simplify the quotient carefully, keep its negative sign, and label a rate as output units per input unit, here °C per minute.

criteria.text: Identifies t = 7 and t = 10 as the bracketing times and sets up (T(10) − T(7))/(10 − 7) = (57 − 65)/3.
criteria.evidence: Response uses the table values at t = 7 and t = 10 in a difference quotient.
criteria.fix: Locate the two table times immediately on either side of 8.5, then form the quotient of their temperature change over their time change.

criteria.text: Obtains T′(8.5) ≈ −8/3 °C per minute.
criteria.evidence: Response states the estimate −8/3 (approximately −2.667).
criteria.fix: Divide −8 by 3 and keep the negative sign; a falling temperature gives a negative rate.

criteria.evidence: Response shows the difference quotient using t = 10 and t = 12 and obtains −2.
criteria.fix: At the last table time, pair it with the previous table time and compute the difference quotient (T(12) − T(10))/(12 − 10).

criteria.text: Explains that T is only defined (and data only given) for 0 ≤ t ≤ 12, so no values after t = 12 exist and the estimate must use an earlier time.
criteria.evidence: Response states that there is no data, or the function is not defined, for t > 12, so only times before 12 can be used.
criteria.fix: Check the domain and table: when a point is at the end of the data, explain that only times on one side are available.

criteria.text: Concludes the temperature is decreasing faster at t = 5, because the estimated rate there has greater magnitude (3.25 > 2 °C per minute, i.e. −3.25 < −2).
criteria.evidence: Response names t = 5 and compares the magnitudes of the two estimates (or notes −3.25 is more negative than −2), consistent with its values from (a) and (c).
criteria.fix: Compare how large the negative rates are: the rate with the greater absolute value means faster decrease. State both values in your justification.

items.title: Sum, Difference, and Constant Multiple Rules for Derivatives
items.stem:
No calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Find f′(x). Then find f′(2).

(b) Find all values of x at which the line tangent to the graph of f is parallel to the line y = 5x + 1. Show the work that leads to your answer.

(c) Find k′(2). Show the work that leads to your answer.

(d) Write an equation for the line tangent to the graph of k at x = 2.
items.stimulus:
Let f be the polynomial function f(x) = 4x³ − 6x² + 5x − 9.

Let g and h be differentiable functions with the following values at x = 2:

x | g(x) | g′(x) | h(x) | h′(x)
2 | 3 | −1 | 5 | 4

The function k is defined by k(x) = 3g(x) − 2h(x) + x³ − 8.
items.answer:
(a) Using the power rule with the constant multiple, sum, and difference rules, and the fact that the derivative of a constant is 0:
f′(x) = 4(3x²) − 6(2x) + 5(1) − 0 = 12x² − 12x + 5.
f′(2) = 12(4) − 12(2) + 5 = 48 − 24 + 5 = 29.

(b) The line y = 5x + 1 has slope 5, and parallel lines have equal slopes, so set f′(x) = 5:
12x² − 12x + 5 = 5
12x² − 12x = 0
12x(x − 1) = 0
x = 0 or x = 1.

(c) By the sum, difference, and constant multiple rules:
k′(x) = 3g′(x) − 2h′(x) + 3x² − 0.
k′(2) = 3(−1) − 2(4) + 3(2)² = −3 − 8 + 12 = 1.

(d) k(2) = 3g(2) − 2h(2) + 2³ − 8 = 3(3) − 2(5) + 8 − 8 = −1.
The slope is k′(2) = 1, so the tangent line is y = −1 + 1(x − 2), which is y = x − 3.

criteria.evidence: Response shows f′(x) = 12x² − 12x + 5, with the constant term −9 differentiating to 0 and each term differentiated with the power rule and constant multiple rule.
criteria.fix: Differentiate term by term: multiply each coefficient by the exponent, lower the exponent by one, and remember a constant's derivative is 0.

criteria.text: Correct value f′(2) = 29
criteria.evidence: Response substitutes x = 2 into its f′(x) and obtains 29, for example 12(4) − 12(2) + 5 = 29. A value consistent with an incorrect f′(x) earns this point.
criteria.fix: Substitute x = 2 into f′(x), not into f(x), and evaluate each term carefully before adding.

criteria.evidence: Response states that parallel lines have equal slopes and writes f′(x) = 5 using its derivative from part (a).
criteria.fix: Parallel tangent lines have the same slope, so set f′(x) equal to the given line's slope and solve.

criteria.text: Correct solutions x = 0 and x = 1
criteria.evidence: Response solves the equation, for example by factoring 12x(x − 1) = 0, and gives both x = 0 and x = 1.
criteria.fix: Factor out the common factor 12x rather than dividing by x, so the solution x = 0 is not lost.

criteria.evidence: Response applies the sum, difference, and constant multiple rules to write k′(x) = 3g′(x) − 2h′(x) + 3x², with the constant −8 differentiating to 0.
criteria.fix: Keep the constant multipliers 3 and −2 in front of g′ and h′; differentiate x³ to 3x² and the constant −8 to 0.

criteria.text: Correct value k′(2) = 1
criteria.evidence: Response substitutes the table values to get 3(−1) − 2(4) + 12 = 1.
criteria.fix: Use the derivative columns g′(2) = −1 and h′(2) = 4, not g(2) and h(2), when evaluating k′(2).

items.stem:
No calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Find f′(x). Then find f′(1).

(b) Use implicit differentiation to find the slope of the curve at the point (1, 2).

(c) Find h′(x). Then find h′(1).
items.stimulus:
Each part below calls for choosing an appropriate combination of differentiation rules.

Let f(x) = x²·e^(3x).

A curve is defined by the equation x² + xy + y² = 7. The point (1, 2) is on the curve.

Let h(x) = arctan(x²).
items.answer:
(a) By the product rule, with the chain rule for e^(3x),
f′(x) = 2x·e^(3x) + x²·3e^(3x) = 2x·e^(3x) + 3x²·e^(3x).
f′(1) = 2e³ + 3e³ = 5e³.

(b) Differentiating x² + xy + y² = 7 with respect to x:
2x + (y + x·dy/dx) + 2y·dy/dx = 0.
At (1, 2): 2 + 2 + 1·dy/dx + 4·dy/dx = 0, so 5·dy/dx = −4 and dy/dx = −4/5. The slope of the curve at (1, 2) is −4/5.

(c) Using d/dx arctan u = u′/(1 + u²) with u = x²,
h′(x) = 2x / (1 + (x²)²) = 2x / (1 + x⁴).
h′(1) = 2/(1 + 1) = 1.

items.title: Counting Caffeine Molecules and Atoms by Mass
items.stem:
A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Calculate the number of moles of caffeine in the tablet.

(b) Calculate the number of caffeine molecules in the tablet.

(c) Calculate the number of nitrogen atoms in the caffeine in the tablet.

(d) The average mass of one caffeine molecule is 194.19 amu. Calculate the average mass of one caffeine molecule in grams.
items.stimulus:
A tablet of a caffeine supplement contains 0.200 g of caffeine, C₈H₁₀N₄O₂. The molar mass of caffeine is 194.19 g/mol, and Avogadro's number is 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.

Answer the following. Report each calculated answer with units and an appropriate number of significant digits.
items.answer:
(a) n = m/M = 0.200 g ÷ 194.19 g/mol = 1.03 × 10⁻³ mol of caffeine.

(b) Number of molecules = 1.03 × 10⁻³ mol × 6.022 × 10²³ molecules/mol = 6.20 × 10²⁰ caffeine molecules.

(c) Each caffeine molecule, C₈H₁₀N₄O₂, contains 4 nitrogen atoms. Number of N atoms = 4 × 6.20 × 10²⁰ = 2.48 × 10²¹ nitrogen atoms.

(d) Because the average mass of one molecule in amu is numerically equal to the molar mass in grams, 1 mol of caffeine (6.022 × 10²³ molecules) has a mass of 194.19 g. Mass of one molecule = 194.19 g/mol ÷ 6.022 × 10²³ molecules/mol = 3.225 × 10⁻²² g.

criteria.text: Calculates 1.03 × 10⁻³ mol of caffeine.
criteria.evidence: Response converts the 0.200 g mass to moles using the molar mass 194.19 g/mol and reports 1.03 × 10⁻³ mol.
criteria.fix: Use n = m/M: divide the mass in grams by the molar mass in g/mol, keeping three significant digits from 0.200 g.

criteria.text: Calculates 6.20 × 10²⁰ caffeine molecules.
criteria.evidence: Response converts the amount of caffeine to a number of molecules with Avogadro's number (for example 1.03 × 10⁻³ mol × 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹) and reports 6.20 × 10²⁰ molecules, or a value consistent with the student's answer to the previous part.
criteria.fix: Multiply the amount in moles by Avogadro's number, 6.022 × 10²³ per mole, to turn moles into a count of molecules.

criteria.text: Calculates 2.48 × 10²¹ nitrogen atoms, using 4 nitrogen atoms per caffeine molecule.
criteria.evidence: Response uses the subscript 4 for N in C₈H₁₀N₄O₂ and reports 2.48 × 10²¹ nitrogen atoms, or 4 times the student's number of molecules from the previous part.
criteria.fix: Read the element's subscript in the formula and multiply the number of molecules by that subscript to count its atoms.

criteria.text: Calculates 3.225 × 10⁻²² g for the mass of one caffeine molecule.
criteria.evidence: Response shows a valid conversion, such as dividing 194.19 g/mol by 6.022 × 10²³ molecules/mol, and reports 3.225 × 10⁻²² g; a difference in the last digit caused by a rounded conversion factor is acceptable.
criteria.fix: The amu mass of one molecule equals the grams in one mole, so divide the molar mass by Avogadro's number to get grams per molecule.

items.title: Identifying an Element from a Two-Isotope Mass Spectrum
items.stem:
A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Calculate the percent abundance of the isotope with mass 62.93 amu.

(b) Calculate the average atomic mass of element X.

(c) Identify element X. Justify your answer.

(d) Atoms of the two isotopes of X have different masses. Explain this difference in terms of the numbers of protons and neutrons in the atoms.
items.stimulus:
A pure sample of an unknown element X is analyzed in a mass spectrometer. Every peak in the spectrum comes from singly charged ions of single atoms of X. The mass of each isotope and the relative intensity of its peak are listed below.

Isotope mass (amu) | Relative intensity
62.93 | 100.0
64.93 | 44.61

Answer the following.
items.answer:
(a) Total intensity = 100.0 + 44.61 = 144.61. Percent abundance of the 62.93 amu isotope = (100.0 ÷ 144.61) × 100% = 69.15%.

(b) The 64.93 amu isotope has an abundance of 100% − 69.15% = 30.85%. Average atomic mass = 0.6915 × 62.93 amu + 0.3085 × 64.93 amu = 43.52 amu + 20.03 amu = 63.55 amu.

(c) X is copper (Cu). The average atomic mass of 63.55 amu matches the atomic mass of copper on the periodic table.

(d) Both isotopes are copper, so every atom of each isotope has 29 protons. The isotope with mass 64.93 amu has two more neutrons (36) than the isotope with mass 62.93 amu (34), and the extra neutrons account for its greater mass.

criteria.text: Calculates a percent abundance of 69.15% for the isotope with mass 62.93 amu.
criteria.evidence: Response divides the intensity of the 62.93 amu peak by the total intensity of both peaks (100.0 ÷ 144.61) and reports 69.15%.
criteria.fix: Add all the peak intensities, then divide the chosen peak's intensity by that total and multiply by 100.

criteria.text: Calculates an average atomic mass of 63.55 amu.
criteria.evidence: Response computes a weighted average of the two isotope masses using their relative abundances or intensities, for example 0.6915 × 62.93 amu + 0.3085 × 64.93 amu, and reports 63.55 amu.
criteria.fix: Weight each isotope mass by its fractional abundance, add the products, and report the result in amu.

criteria.text: Identifies X as copper (Cu) because the calculated average atomic mass, 63.55 amu, matches the atomic mass of copper on the periodic table.
criteria.evidence: Response names copper and links the average atomic mass from the previous part to the atomic mass listed for Cu.
criteria.fix: Compare your calculated average atomic mass with the periodic table and name the element whose atomic mass matches it.

criteria.text: Explains that atoms of both isotopes have the same number of protons (29) but atoms of the heavier isotope have 2 more neutrons.
criteria.evidence: Response states that the number of protons is the same in both isotopes (they are the same element) and that the 64.93 amu isotope has more neutrons (two more); it does not attribute the mass difference to protons or electrons.
criteria.fix: Isotopes of one element always share the same number of protons; explain any mass difference by a different number of neutrons.

items.title: Interpreting the Photoelectron Spectrum of an Unknown Element
items.stem:
No calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Using the data in the table, write the complete ground-state electron configuration of element X and identify the element. Explain how the relative peak heights support your answer.

(b) The binding energy of peak 1 (210 MJ/mol) is much greater than that of peak 4 (1.95 MJ/mol). Explain this difference in terms of the interactions between the electrons and the nucleus.

(c) A photoelectron spectrum of sulfur (atomic number 16) is obtained under the same conditions. Identify the relative height of the sulfur peak with the lowest binding energy, and justify your answer using the electron configuration of sulfur.

(d) Predict whether the 1s peak of sulfur appears at a binding energy greater than, less than, or equal to 210 MJ/mol. Justify your prediction in terms of the interactions between the electrons and the nucleus.
items.stimulus:
A student obtains the photoelectron spectrum of a gaseous sample of an unknown element X. All atoms are in the ground state. The spectrum shows five peaks. The binding energy of each peak and its relative peak height are listed below.

Peak | Binding energy (MJ/mol) | Relative peak height
1 | 210 | 2
2 | 18.7 | 2
3 | 13.5 | 6
4 | 1.95 | 2
5 | 1.06 | 3

Answer the following.
items.answer:
(a) In PES, the relative height of each peak is proportional to the number of electrons in that subshell. Assigning subshells from highest to lowest binding energy: peak 1 = 1s (2 electrons), peak 2 = 2s (2), peak 3 = 2p (6), peak 4 = 3s (2), peak 5 = 3p (3). The configuration is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p³. The total is 2 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 3 = 15 electrons, so a neutral atom has 15 protons and X is phosphorus.

(b) Peak 1 corresponds to 1s electrons and peak 4 to 3s electrons. The 1s electrons are in the first shell, much closer to the nucleus, and have no inner electrons shielding them, so they experience a much greater effective nuclear charge. By Coulomb's law, the attraction between the nucleus and the 1s electrons is much stronger than for the 3s electrons, which are farther away and shielded by the 10 electrons in the first and second shells. Therefore much more energy is required to remove a 1s electron.

(c) Sulfur has 16 electrons, with configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁴. The peak with the lowest binding energy corresponds to the 3p subshell, which holds 4 electrons, so its relative height is 4.

(d) The sulfur 1s peak appears at a binding energy greater than 210 MJ/mol. Sulfur has 16 protons compared with 15 for phosphorus, while its 1s electrons are still in the first shell at a similar distance and with no shielding. The greater nuclear charge attracts the 1s electrons more strongly, so more energy is needed to remove them.

criteria.text: Gives the configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p³ and identifies X as phosphorus (P), using the peak heights as electron counts.
criteria.evidence: States the full configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p³, names phosphorus, and explains that each relative peak height equals the number of electrons in that subshell, totaling 15 electrons.
criteria.fix: Treat each relative peak height as the electron count in a subshell, assign subshells from highest to lowest binding energy, then sum electrons.

criteria.text: Explains that 1s electrons are much closer to the nucleus and experience little shielding, so the Coulombic attraction to the nucleus is much stronger than for 3s electrons.
criteria.evidence: Identifies peak 1 as 1s and peak 4 as 3s, and states that the 1s electrons are closer to the nucleus (smaller distance) and less shielded (greater effective nuclear charge), giving greater Coulombic attraction and requiring more energy to remove.
criteria.fix: Use Coulomb's law: compare distance from the nucleus and shielding by inner electrons for each subshell, then link stronger attraction to larger binding energy.

criteria.text: States the lowest-energy (3p) peak of sulfur has a relative height of 4 because sulfur's configuration is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁴.
criteria.evidence: Gives a relative height of 4 for the lowest binding energy peak and supports it with the configuration ending in 3p⁴ (four 3p electrons).
criteria.fix: Write the configuration of the new element first, then match the lowest binding energy peak to its outermost subshell and count those electrons.

criteria.text: Predicts the sulfur 1s peak is at a binding energy greater than 210 MJ/mol because sulfur has one more proton, giving greater nuclear charge and stronger attraction for 1s electrons.
criteria.evidence: Claims greater than 210 MJ/mol and justifies it by sulfur's larger nuclear charge (16 protons versus 15) attracting the 1s electrons, which are in the same shell and essentially unshielded, more strongly.
criteria.fix: For the same subshell in two elements, compare the number of protons; more protons means greater Coulombic attraction and a higher binding energy.

items.title: Ionization Energy and Ionic Radius Trends in Groups
items.stem:
No calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) The first ionization energy decreases going down Group 2 from Be to Ba. Explain this trend in terms of the electronic structure of the atoms and Coulomb's law.

(b) Estimate the first ionization energy of Sr. Show how you obtained your estimate and justify why your value is reasonable based on periodic trends.

(c) Although Al has one more proton than Mg, the first ionization energy of Al is lower than that of Mg. Explain this observation in terms of the electron configurations of the two atoms.

(d) The ions Na⁺ and Mg²⁺ both have the electron configuration 1s²2s²2p⁶. Identify which ion has the smaller radius and justify your answer.
items.stimulus:
A student collects the first ionization energies of several main-group elements from a reference table. The value for strontium, Sr, is missing from the student's source.

Element | Group | Period | First ionization energy (kJ/mol)
Na | 1 | 3 | 496
Mg | 2 | 3 | 738
Al | 13 | 3 | 578
Be | 2 | 2 | 900
Ca | 2 | 4 | 590
Sr | 2 | 5 | (missing)
Ba | 2 | 6 | 503

Answer the following using the data and your knowledge of atomic structure.
items.answer:
(a) All Group 2 atoms have two valence electrons in an s subshell, but going down the group from Be to Ba each atom has an additional occupied shell. The valence electron is therefore farther from the nucleus and more shielded by the inner (core) electrons. The effective nuclear charge felt by the valence electron stays about the same, and by Coulomb's law the attractive force decreases as distance increases. Because the valence electron is held less strongly, less energy is required to remove it, so the first ionization energy decreases from Be to Ba.

(b) Sr lies between Ca and Ba in Group 2, so its first ionization energy should fall between their values. Averaging: (590 + 503)/2 = 546.5, so about 547 kJ/mol. This is reasonable because Sr's valence electron (5s) is farther from the nucleus than Ca's (4s) but closer than Ba's (6s), so its ionization energy should be lower than 590 kJ/mol and higher than 503 kJ/mol.

(c) Mg is [Ne]3s² and Al is [Ne]3s²3p¹. The electron removed from Mg comes from the 3s subshell, while the electron removed from Al is the single 3p electron. The 3p electron is higher in energy and is partially shielded from the nucleus by the 3s electrons, so it experiences a weaker attraction even though Al has one more proton. Less energy is needed to remove it, so Al has a lower first ionization energy than Mg.

(d) Mg²⁺ has the smaller radius. Both ions have 10 electrons in the same two shells, so shielding is about the same, but Mg²⁺ has 12 protons while Na⁺ has 11. The greater nuclear charge of Mg²⁺ attracts the electrons more strongly and pulls them closer to the nucleus, making Mg²⁺ smaller.

criteria.fix: Connect each additional occupied shell to greater electron-nucleus distance, then use Coulomb's law to state the attraction weakens, lowering ionization energy.

criteria.text: Gives an estimate strictly between 503 kJ/mol and 590 kJ/mol (for example, the average of Ca and Ba, about 547 kJ/mol), justified by Sr lying between Ca and Ba in Group 2.
criteria.evidence: Response reports a numerical value greater than 503 and less than 590 kJ/mol with a stated basis, such as averaging the Ca and Ba values or noting Sr is between Ca and Ba in the group trend.
criteria.fix: Locate the missing element between its group neighbors, then choose a value between their ionization energies, for example by averaging them.

criteria.text: Explains that the electron removed from Al is a 3p electron, which is higher in energy (farther from the nucleus on average) and partially shielded by the 3s electrons, whereas the electron removed from Mg comes from the filled 3s subshell.
criteria.evidence: Response identifies the electron removed from Al as 3p and from Mg as 3s, and states that the 3p electron is shielded by the 3s electrons or is higher in energy, so it is held less tightly despite the greater nuclear charge.
criteria.fix: Write both electron configurations, identify which subshell loses the electron, and explain the 3p electron is shielded by 3s electrons.

criteria.text: Identifies Mg²⁺ as the smaller ion, because with the same number of electrons in the same shells Mg²⁺ has more protons (12 versus 11), so the greater nuclear charge pulls the electrons closer.
criteria.evidence: Response states Mg²⁺ is smaller and justifies it with the greater nuclear charge (more protons or greater effective nuclear charge) acting on the same number of electrons in the same shells.

items.title: Predicting Ionic Formulas from Periodic Table Position
items.stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Predict the formula of the ionic compound formed from barium and bromine. Justify your prediction using the positions of the elements on the periodic table.

(b) Predict the formula of the ionic compound formed from potassium and sulfur. Justify your prediction.

(c) Predict the formula of the ionic compound formed from aluminum and oxygen. Justify your prediction in terms of the number of valence electrons in each atom.

(d) Potassium reacts with chlorine more vigorously than sodium does. Explain this difference in terms of the interactions between the valence electron and the nucleus in each atom.
items.stimulus: Magnesium and chlorine form the ionic compound MgCl₂. Sodium and oxygen form the ionic compound Na₂O. Use these formulas and the periodic table to answer the following.
items.answer:
(a) BaBr₂. Barium is in group 2 with magnesium, and bromine is in group 17 with chlorine. Elements in the same column form analogous compounds, so barium and bromine form BaBr₂, just as magnesium and chlorine form MgCl₂ (Ba²⁺ and Br⁻ ions).

(b) K₂S. Potassium is in group 1 with sodium, and sulfur is in group 16 with oxygen, so the compound is analogous to Na₂O, with K⁺ and S²⁻ ions.

(c) Al₂O₃. An aluminum atom has 3 valence electrons and loses them to form Al³⁺. An oxygen atom has 6 valence electrons and gains 2 to form O²⁻. Two Al³⁺ ions (+6) balance three O²⁻ ions (−6), giving Al₂O₃.

(d) The valence electron of potassium is in the fourth shell, while that of sodium is in the third shell. The potassium valence electron is farther from the nucleus and is shielded by more inner electrons, so by Coulomb's law it is attracted less strongly to the nucleus. It is therefore removed more easily, so potassium forms K⁺ and reacts with chlorine more readily than sodium does.

criteria.evidence: Response gives BaBr₂ and justifies it by group membership (Ba with Mg in group 2, Br with Cl in group 17), or by the typical charges Ba²⁺ and Br⁻ that follow from those positions.
criteria.fix: Locate each element's column; elements in the same columns as those in a known compound form a compound with an analogous formula.

criteria.evidence: Response gives K₂S and justifies it by group membership (K with Na in group 1, S with O in group 16), or by the typical charges K⁺ and S²⁻.
criteria.fix: Match potassium to sodium and sulfur to oxygen by column, then use the same subscripts as the known compound Na₂O.

criteria.text: Predicts Al₂O₃ because aluminum (3 valence electrons) forms Al³⁺ and oxygen (6 valence electrons) forms O²⁻, and 2(+3) + 3(−2) = 0.
criteria.evidence: Response gives Al₂O₃, states the charges +3 and −2 based on losing 3 or gaining 2 valence electrons, and shows that the charges balance.
criteria.fix: Get each ion's charge from the valence electrons lost or gained to reach a noble-gas configuration, then choose subscripts giving zero total charge.

criteria.text: Explains that potassium's valence electron is in a higher shell (n = 4 rather than n = 3), farther from the nucleus and more shielded, so it is attracted less strongly and is lost more easily when potassium forms an ionic compound.
criteria.evidence: Response states that the K valence electron is farther from the nucleus (or in a higher shell) than the Na valence electron and links this to a weaker Coulombic attraction, making it easier to remove.
criteria.fix: Compare the shell that holds each valence electron; a farther, more shielded electron feels weaker attraction and is lost more easily.

items.title: Bond Polarity from Electronegativity Values
items.stem:
A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Classify the C–H bond as nonpolar covalent or polar covalent. Justify your answer.

(b) In an N–H bond, identify the atom that carries the partial negative charge. Justify your answer.

(c) C–O and C–F are both single bonds. Identify which of these two bonds has the larger bond dipole. Justify your answer using the data.

(d) Fluorine has a greater electronegativity than chlorine. Explain this difference using the shell model and Coulomb's law.
items.stimulus:
The table lists Pauling electronegativity values for several elements.

Element | Electronegativity
H | 2.20
C | 2.55
N | 3.04
O | 3.44
F | 3.98
Cl | 3.16

Answer the following about covalent bonds between these elements.
items.answer:
(a) Nonpolar covalent. The electronegativity difference is 2.55 − 2.20 = 0.35, which is small, so carbon and hydrogen share the bonding electrons nearly equally and the C–H bond is effectively nonpolar.

(b) Nitrogen carries the partial negative charge. Nitrogen (3.04) is more electronegative than hydrogen (2.20), so the shared electrons are pulled closer to the N atom.

(c) C–F has the larger bond dipole. The electronegativity difference for C–F is 3.98 − 2.55 = 1.43, while for C–O it is 3.44 − 2.55 = 0.89. For single bonds, a greater electronegativity difference gives a greater bond dipole.

(d) The valence electrons of fluorine are in the second shell, while those of chlorine are in the third shell. Both atoms have the same core charge (+7) acting on their valence shell, but the shared electrons in a bond to fluorine are much closer to its nucleus. By Coulomb's law, the smaller distance gives a stronger attraction, so fluorine attracts shared electrons more strongly and has the greater electronegativity.

criteria.evidence: Response states nonpolar covalent and cites the small electronegativity difference, 0.35, or nearly equal sharing of the bonding electrons.
criteria.fix: Subtract the two electronegativities; a small difference, as in C–H, means nearly equal sharing, so treat the bond as nonpolar covalent.

criteria.text: Identifies nitrogen as the atom with the partial negative charge because N is more electronegative than H (3.04 versus 2.20).
criteria.evidence: Response names nitrogen and justifies it by nitrogen's higher electronegativity, which pulls the shared electrons toward the N atom.
criteria.fix: Compare the two electronegativities; the more electronegative atom pulls the shared electrons toward itself and carries the partial negative charge.

criteria.text: Identifies C–F as having the larger bond dipole because its electronegativity difference (1.43) is greater than that of C–O (0.89).
criteria.evidence: Response names C–F and supports the choice with the two differences, 1.43 and 0.89, or with the statement that F is more electronegative than O so the C–F difference is larger.
criteria.fix: Calculate the electronegativity difference for each single bond; the bond with the larger difference has the larger bond dipole.

items.title: Potential Energy Curve for Cl2 and Ionic Interactions
items.stem:
A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Using the data in the table, identify the equilibrium bond length of the Cl–Cl bond. Justify your answer.

(b) Calculate the bond energy of the Cl–Cl bond in kJ/mol. Show your work and report your answer with the correct number of significant figures.

(c) At an internuclear distance of 150 pm, the potential energy is positive. Explain this observation in terms of the interactions between the particles in the two atoms.

(d) Carbon monoxide, CO, contains a carbon-oxygen triple bond, while each carbon-oxygen bond in carbon dioxide, CO2, is a double bond. Predict which molecule has the shorter carbon-oxygen bond and the larger carbon-oxygen bond energy. Justify your prediction.

(e) Solid MgO contains Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ ions, and solid NaF contains Na⁺ and F⁻ ions. The distances between the centers of adjacent cations and anions in the two solids are similar. Identify which compound has the stronger attraction between its cations and anions, and justify your answer using Coulomb's law.
items.stimulus:
A student uses a computer model to calculate the potential energy of two chlorine atoms as a function of the distance between their nuclei (internuclear distance). The potential energy is defined as zero when the atoms are infinitely far apart. Selected results are shown in the table.

Internuclear distance (pm) | Potential energy per pair of atoms (×10⁻¹⁹ J)
150 | +3.10
170 | −2.20
185 | −3.65
199 | −4.02
215 | −3.80
250 | −2.60
300 | −1.20
400 | −0.25
infinite | 0

Avogadro's number is 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.
items.answer:
(a) The equilibrium bond length is 199 pm. At this distance the potential energy is at its minimum value, −4.02 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, so the two atoms are most stable at this separation.

(b) The bond energy is the energy needed to separate the atoms from the minimum (−4.02 × 10⁻¹⁹ J) to zero, so 4.02 × 10⁻¹⁹ J per bond.
(4.02 × 10⁻¹⁹ J/bond)(6.022 × 10²³ bonds/mol) = 2.42 × 10⁵ J/mol
2.42 × 10⁵ J/mol × (1 kJ / 1000 J) = 242 kJ/mol

(c) At 150 pm the atoms are much closer than the equilibrium bond length. At this short distance the repulsion between the two positively charged nuclei, and between the electrons of the two atoms, becomes greater than the attraction of each nucleus for the electrons of the other atom. Because repulsion dominates, the potential energy is higher than that of the separated atoms, so it is positive.

(d) CO has the shorter carbon-oxygen bond and the larger carbon-oxygen bond energy. The C–O bond in CO is a triple bond (bond order 3), while each C–O bond in CO2 is a double bond (bond order 2). More shared electron pairs between the same two atoms pull the nuclei closer together and hold them more strongly, so a higher bond order gives a shorter bond with a larger bond energy.

(e) MgO has the stronger attraction. By Coulomb's law, the force between ions is proportional to q₁q₂/r². The distances are similar, but the ion charges in MgO (2+ and 2−) are larger than those in NaF (1+ and 1−), so the product of the charges is four times as large in magnitude, giving a stronger attraction in MgO.

criteria.text: Identifies the equilibrium bond length as 199 pm because the potential energy is lowest (most negative, −4.02 × 10⁻¹⁹ J) at that distance.
criteria.evidence: States 199 pm and links it to the minimum potential energy in the table.
criteria.fix: Find the internuclear distance where potential energy is lowest; that minimum defines the equilibrium bond length.

criteria.text: Calculates the bond energy as 242 kJ/mol from 4.02 × 10⁻¹⁹ J per bond multiplied by Avogadro's number and converted to kJ.
criteria.evidence: Shows (4.02 × 10⁻¹⁹ J)(6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹) = 2.42 × 10⁵ J/mol and converts to 242 kJ/mol, reported to three significant figures as a positive value.
criteria.fix: Take the depth of the minimum as energy per bond, multiply by Avogadro's number, divide by 1000, and keep three significant figures.

criteria.text: Explains that at 150 pm the atoms are closer than the equilibrium distance, so repulsions between the two positively charged nuclei (and between the electron clouds) dominate over the attractions of each nucleus for the other atom's electrons.
criteria.evidence: Identifies nucleus–nucleus (or electron–electron) repulsion as exceeding nucleus–electron attraction at short distance.
criteria.fix: At very short distances, describe nucleus–nucleus repulsion becoming larger than nucleus–electron attraction, which raises the potential energy.

criteria.text: Predicts that CO has the shorter carbon-oxygen bond and the larger bond energy, justified by its higher bond order (triple versus double).
criteria.evidence: Chooses CO for both shorter length and larger bond energy and cites bond order 3 versus 2 (more shared electron pairs between the same two atoms).
criteria.fix: Compare bond orders between the same two atoms: higher bond order means shorter bond and larger bond energy.

criteria.text: Identifies MgO as having the stronger cation–anion attraction because, by Coulomb's law, interaction strength is proportional to the product of the ion charges (2+ and 2− versus 1+ and 1−) at similar internuclear distance.
criteria.evidence: Chooses MgO and refers to the larger ion charges in MgO increasing the Coulombic attraction, with distance being similar.
criteria.fix: Apply Coulomb's law F ∝ q₁q₂/r²: when distances are similar, compare ion charges; larger charges give stronger attraction.

items.title: Particulate Models and Coulombic Forces in NaCl and MgO
items.stem:
A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) A student proposes a different particulate model for one layer of solid NaCl. In it, each Na+ ion has two Na+ ions and two Cl− ions as its nearest neighbors in the layer. The accepted model has only oppositely charged ions as nearest neighbors. Explain why the accepted model is more consistent with Coulomb's law than the student's model.

(b) Using the ionic radii, determine the distance between the centers of adjacent Na+ and Cl− ions and between the centers of adjacent Mg2+ and O2− ions. Then calculate the ratio of the magnitude of the Coulombic attraction for one Mg2+–O2− pair to that for one Na+–Cl− pair. Show your work.

(c) Explain, in terms of the particulate model and Coulombic attractions, why MgO has a much higher melting point than NaCl.

(d) A crystal of NaCl shatters when struck sharply with a hammer. Use the particulate model of the ionic array to explain this behavior.
items.stimulus:
Sodium chloride, NaCl, and magnesium oxide, MgO, are ionic solids. In each crystal the ions are arranged in a repeating three-dimensional array. Every cation is surrounded by six nearest-neighbor anions, and every anion is surrounded by six nearest-neighbor cations. Treat the ions as hard spheres that touch their nearest neighbors. The magnitude of the Coulombic attraction between a cation and an anion is proportional to |q1q2|/r², where r is the distance between the ion centers.

Ion | Ionic radius (pm)
Na+ | 102
Mg2+ | 72
Cl− | 181
O2− | 140

Substance | Melting point (°C)
NaCl | 801
MgO | 2852
items.answer:
(a) In the accepted model, every Na+ is touching only Cl− ions and every Cl− is touching only Na+ ions. By Coulomb's law, opposite charges at short distance attract strongly, so this arrangement maximizes attractive forces. Ions of the same charge are never nearest neighbors, so they stay farther apart and repulsions are minimized. In the student's model, Na+ ions sit next to other Na+ ions at short distance, which produces strong repulsions and fewer attractions. That arrangement would be higher in energy and less stable.

(b) The ions touch, so distance = cation radius + anion radius.
Na+–Cl−: 102 pm + 181 pm = 283 pm
Mg2+–O2−: 72 pm + 140 pm = 212 pm
Ratio = (|2 × −2| / 212²) ÷ (|1 × −1| / 283²) = 4 × (283/212)² = 4 × 1.782 = 7.13
The attraction for one Mg2+–O2− pair is about 7.13 times that for one Na+–Cl− pair.

(c) The ions in MgO have charges of 2+ and 2−, compared with 1+ and 1− in NaCl. They are also closer together (212 pm versus 283 pm). Both factors make the Coulombic attractions in the MgO array much stronger. Melting requires overcoming these attractions so the ions can move past one another. Much more energy is needed for MgO, so its melting point is much higher.

(d) A sharp blow shifts one plane of ions relative to the plane next to it by about one ion position. After the shift, Na+ ions lie next to Na+ ions and Cl− ions lie next to Cl− ions. The strong repulsions between these like charges push the two planes apart, so the crystal breaks cleanly along that plane instead of bending.

criteria.text: States that in the accepted model each ion's nearest neighbors are oppositely charged, maximizing cation–anion attractions, while like-charged ions are kept farther apart, minimizing repulsions.
criteria.evidence: Response must refer to both attraction between nearest-neighbor opposite charges and reduced repulsion from like charges being farther apart. It must also state or imply that the student's model places like charges at short distance, causing strong repulsion.
criteria.fix: Explain both effects: adjacent opposite charges maximize attraction, and keeping like charges farther apart minimizes repulsion, giving a lower-energy arrangement.

criteria.text: Correct internuclear distances: 283 pm for Na+–Cl− and 212 pm for Mg2+–O2−, each found by adding the cation and anion radii.
criteria.evidence: Response must show the sums 102 + 181 = 283 pm and 72 + 140 = 212 pm, with units.
criteria.fix: For touching spheres, add the cation radius and the anion radius to get the center-to-center distance, and include units.

criteria.text: Correct ratio of attraction magnitudes, about 7.13, from (2×2/212²) ÷ (1×1/283²).
criteria.evidence: Response must set up the ratio using the charge products (4 and 1) and the squared distances from part (b). It must report a value of about 7.13. An error carried forward from incorrect distances earns credit if the setup is correct.
criteria.fix: Write |q1q2|/r² for each pair, divide MgO's value by NaCl's, and square the distances before dividing.

criteria.text: MgO ions attract each other more strongly, because they have larger charges and a smaller internuclear distance. More energy is therefore needed to overcome the attractions holding ions in the array, giving a higher melting point.
criteria.evidence: Response must cite the larger charges (2+/2−) and/or the smaller distance as the cause of stronger Coulombic attraction. It must link that stronger attraction to more energy being needed to separate the ions during melting.
criteria.fix: Connect ion charge and size to attraction strength, then state that stronger attractions require more energy to disrupt the ionic array during melting.

criteria.text: Striking the crystal shifts one layer of ions relative to the next, so that like-charged ions become nearest neighbors. The resulting strong repulsions push the layers apart, and the crystal cleaves.
criteria.evidence: Response must describe the displacement of a layer or plane of ions. It must state that like charges are brought next to each other and that the resulting repulsion causes the crystal to break.
criteria.fix: Describe what happens when ion layers slide: like charges line up next to each other, and their repulsion splits the crystal.

items.title: Classifying Alloys of Copper, Silver, and Iron by Atomic Radius
items.stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Describe a particle-level model of pure solid copper that shows the essential features of metallic bonding.

(b) Classify cupronickel as a substitutional alloy or an interstitial alloy, and describe where the nickel atoms are located. Justify your answer using the data.

(c) Classify nitrided iron as a substitutional alloy or an interstitial alloy, and describe where the nitrogen atoms are located. Justify your answer using the data.

(d) A student claims that sterling silver must be an interstitial alloy because copper atoms are smaller than silver atoms. Evaluate the student's claim using the data.
items.stimulus:
Approximate atomic radii of five elements are listed below.

Element | Atomic radius (pm)
Cu | 128
Ni | 124
Ag | 144
Fe | 126
N | 71

Cupronickel, used in some coins, is an alloy of copper and nickel. Nitrided iron is an alloy of iron that contains a small amount of nitrogen. Sterling silver is an alloy of silver and copper. Answer the following.
items.answer:
(a) Solid copper is a regular three-dimensional array of positive copper ions. The valence electrons are not attached to any one ion; they are delocalized and move freely throughout the whole solid as a sea of electrons that holds the cations together.

(b) Cupronickel is a substitutional alloy. The radii of Cu (128 pm) and Ni (124 pm) are very similar, so nickel atoms can take the place of copper atoms at positions in the copper lattice.

(c) Nitrided iron is an interstitial alloy. A nitrogen atom (71 pm) is much smaller than an iron atom (126 pm), so the nitrogen atoms fit into the spaces between the iron atoms while the iron atoms keep their lattice positions.

(d) The claim is incorrect. Copper atoms (128 pm) are only about 11% smaller than silver atoms (144 pm), so the radii are comparable. Copper atoms therefore replace silver atoms at lattice positions, and sterling silver is a substitutional alloy. An interstitial alloy forms only when one atom is much smaller than the other, as with N (71 pm) in Fe (126 pm).

criteria.text: Describes an array of positive copper ions surrounded by delocalized valence electrons (a sea of electrons) that are not associated with any single ion.
criteria.evidence: Response states that solid copper consists of copper cations arranged in a regular array and that the valence electrons are delocalized throughout the solid rather than bound to individual atoms.
criteria.fix: Describe two features: copper cations held in a regular array, and valence electrons spread through the whole solid rather than belonging to one atom.

criteria.text: Classifies cupronickel as a substitutional alloy in which nickel atoms take the place of copper atoms at positions in the lattice, because Cu (128 pm) and Ni (124 pm) have comparable radii.
criteria.evidence: Response states substitutional, says that Ni atoms replace (substitute for) Cu atoms in the lattice, and supports this by noting that the two radii are similar.
criteria.fix: Compare the two radii; atoms of similar size can replace one another at lattice positions, which defines a substitutional alloy.

criteria.text: Classifies nitrided iron as an interstitial alloy in which nitrogen atoms occupy the spaces between iron atoms, because N (71 pm) is much smaller than Fe (126 pm).
criteria.evidence: Response states interstitial, says the N atoms fill spaces (interstices) between Fe atoms in the lattice, and supports this by noting that the N radius is much smaller than the Fe radius.
criteria.fix: When one atom is much smaller, it fits into the gaps between the larger atoms; name this an interstitial alloy and cite the radii.

criteria.text: States that the claim is incorrect: Cu (128 pm) is only slightly smaller than Ag (144 pm), so the radii are comparable and copper substitutes for silver, making sterling silver a substitutional alloy; interstitial alloys require a much smaller atom, as with N (71 pm) in Fe (126 pm).
criteria.evidence: Response rejects the claim and explains that the Ag and Cu radii are comparable (differing by only about 11%), so sterling silver is substitutional; being merely smaller is not enough for an interstitial alloy.
criteria.fix: Judge how large the size difference is, not just which atom is smaller; only a much smaller atom fits between atoms of the host metal.

items.title: Lewis Structures of Acetonitrile and Methyl Isocyanide
items.stem:
No calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Using the data in the table, calculate the total number of valence electrons that must appear in a Lewis structure of CH3CN. Show your work.

(b) Describe in words a complete Lewis structure for CH3CN in which every carbon and nitrogen atom has an octet. State every bond with its type and the number of lone pairs on each atom.

(c) A student proposes a Lewis structure for CH3CN with only single bonds (three C–H, one C–C, one C–N) and three lone pairs on the nitrogen atom. This structure contains 16 valence electrons. Explain why this structure is not acceptable, referring to the electrons around a specific atom.

(d) Describe in words a Lewis structure for methyl isocyanide, CH3NC, in which every carbon and nitrogen atom has an octet. State every bond with its type and the number of lone pairs on each atom.
items.stimulus:
Acetonitrile, CH3CN, is a common laboratory solvent. Its atoms are connected as follows: a carbon atom (the methyl carbon) is bonded to three hydrogen atoms and to a second carbon atom, and the second carbon atom is bonded to the nitrogen atom. Its isomer, methyl isocyanide, CH3NC, has the same molecular formula but different connectivity: the methyl carbon is bonded to three hydrogen atoms and to the nitrogen atom, and the nitrogen atom is bonded to a terminal carbon atom.

Element | Valence electrons per atom | Atoms in one CH3CN molecule
C | 4 | 2
H | 1 | 3
N | 5 | 1

Because answers are typed, describe each Lewis structure in words: state each bond and whether it is single, double or triple, and state the number of lone pairs on each atom.
items.answer:
(a) Valence electrons = (2 C)(4) + (3 H)(1) + (1 N)(5) = 8 + 3 + 5 = 16 valence electrons.

(b) The methyl carbon forms three C–H single bonds and one C–C single bond. The second carbon forms that C–C single bond and a C≡N triple bond. Nitrogen has one lone pair; neither carbon has any lone pairs, and the hydrogens have none. Check: bonds use (3 + 1 + 3) × 2 = 14 electrons, plus 2 in the lone pair = 16. Each carbon has 4 bonding pairs (8 electrons) and nitrogen has 3 bonding pairs + 1 lone pair (8 electrons). Written compactly: H3C–C≡N: with the lone pair on N.

(c) In the student's structure the carbon bonded to nitrogen has only two single bonds (C–C and C–N) and no lone pairs, so it is surrounded by only 4 electrons instead of an octet. Converting two of the lone pairs on nitrogen into bonding pairs between C and N gives the triple bond and an octet on both atoms, so the all-single-bond structure is not acceptable.

(d) CH3NC also has 16 valence electrons. The methyl carbon forms three C–H single bonds and a C–N single bond. Nitrogen forms that C–N single bond and an N≡C triple bond to the terminal carbon, and has no lone pairs (4 bonding pairs = 8 electrons). The terminal carbon has the triple bond plus one lone pair (8 electrons). Methyl carbon: 4 bonding pairs = 8 electrons. Total: 7 bonding pairs (14 electrons) + 1 lone pair (2 electrons) = 16. Compactly: H3C–N≡C: with the lone pair on the terminal C.

criteria.text: Total valence electrons = 16, from 2(4) + 3(1) + 1(5).
criteria.evidence: Shows the sum of valence electrons for each element times the number of atoms and reports 16.
criteria.fix: Multiply each element's valence electrons by its atom count, then add: carbon 2 × 4, hydrogen 3 × 1, nitrogen 1 × 5.

criteria.text: Bonds: three C–H single bonds, one C–C single bond, and one C≡N triple bond.
criteria.evidence: States each of the three C–H bonds and the C–C bond as single and the carbon-nitrogen bond as triple.
criteria.fix: After placing single bonds, check each atom's octet; if the electrons run short, convert lone pairs into extra bonding pairs between neighbors.

criteria.text: Lone pairs: one lone pair on N, zero lone pairs on either carbon, giving each C and N an octet and 16 electrons in total.
criteria.evidence: States one lone pair on nitrogen and no lone pairs on either carbon (hydrogens have none), consistent with octets and 16 total electrons.
criteria.fix: Count bonding plus lone-pair electrons around each atom, confirm 8 for C and N, and confirm the grand total matches the valence count.

criteria.text: The second (central) carbon has only two bonding pairs, 4 electrons, so it lacks an octet; the structure must be rejected.
criteria.evidence: Identifies the carbon bonded to nitrogen and states it is surrounded by only 4 electrons (fewer than 8), violating the octet rule.
criteria.fix: Tally the electrons around every non-hydrogen atom in a proposed structure; any carbon with fewer than 8 electrons signals missing multiple bonds.
variants: carbon bonded to N has only two bonds

criteria.text: H3C–N≡C: three C–H single bonds, a C–N single bond, an N≡C triple bond, zero lone pairs on N, one lone pair on the terminal C, none on the methyl C.
criteria.evidence: Gives the single and triple bonds with the triple bond between N and the terminal carbon, places the one lone pair on the terminal carbon and none on nitrogen.
criteria.fix: Keep 16 electrons for the isomer, place the triple bond between N and terminal C, then put the leftover pair where an octet is incomplete.

items.title: Matching Absorption Regions to Transitions in Carbon Monoxide
items.stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Identify the type of transition in a CO molecule that is associated with absorption 1.

(b) Identify the type of transition in a CO molecule that is associated with absorption 2.

(c) A student claims that absorption 3 makes the C–O bond vibrate more energetically. Evaluate the student's claim.

(d) A sample of argon gas, which consists of separate argon atoms, absorbs no microwave or infrared radiation. Explain this observation.
items.stimulus:
A gaseous sample of carbon monoxide, CO, is studied with three different spectrometers. Each absorption the sample shows is listed below with the region of the electromagnetic spectrum in which it occurs.

Absorption | Region | Wavelength
1 | microwave | 2.60 mm
2 | infrared | 4.67 μm
3 | ultraviolet | 155 nm

Answer the following.
items.answer:
(a) Absorption 1 is in the microwave region, which is associated with transitions between rotational energy levels. Absorbing the photon moves the CO molecule to a higher rotational energy level.

(b) Absorption 2 is in the infrared region, which is associated with transitions between vibrational energy levels. Absorbing the photon moves the molecule to a higher vibrational energy level, so the C–O bond vibrates more energetically.

(c) The claim is incorrect. Absorption 3 is in the ultraviolet region, which is associated with electronic transitions: the photon promotes an electron in the molecule to a higher electronic energy level. Changes in bond vibration are associated with infrared radiation, not ultraviolet radiation.

(d) Microwave absorption requires transitions between molecular rotational levels, and infrared absorption requires transitions between molecular vibrational levels. Argon exists as separate atoms with no chemical bonds, so there is no bond to vibrate and no molecular rotation to change. With no such transitions available, argon does not absorb microwave or infrared radiation; it can absorb only at energies that cause electronic transitions.

criteria.text: Identifies a transition between rotational energy levels of the molecule.
criteria.evidence: Response states that the microwave absorption corresponds to a change in the molecule's rotational energy level (the molecule rotating faster).
criteria.fix: Memorize the pairings: microwave with rotational levels, infrared with vibrational levels, ultraviolet or visible with electronic energy levels.

criteria.text: Identifies a transition between vibrational energy levels of the molecule.
criteria.evidence: Response states that the infrared absorption corresponds to a change in the vibrational energy level of the C–O bond (the bond vibrating more energetically).
criteria.fix: Link infrared radiation to bond vibrations: an absorbed infrared photon moves the molecule to a higher vibrational energy level.

criteria.text: States that the claim is incorrect because ultraviolet absorption corresponds to an electronic transition, in which an electron moves to a higher electronic energy level, not a vibrational transition.
criteria.evidence: Response rejects the claim and identifies absorption 3 as an electronic transition (an electron promoted to a higher energy level).
criteria.fix: Match the claim's spectral region to its transition before agreeing; ultraviolet radiation changes electronic energy levels, while vibrations are changed by infrared.

criteria.text: Explains that argon atoms are not bonded to other atoms, so there are no molecular rotational or vibrational transitions available to absorb microwave or infrared radiation.
criteria.evidence: Response states that a single atom has no bond to vibrate and no molecular rotation, and connects this to the absence of microwave (rotational) and infrared (vibrational) absorption.
criteria.fix: Ask what each region changes: rotation and vibration transitions need a molecule with bonded atoms, which a separate argon atom lacks.

items.title: Molar Volumes of Argon in the Solid, Liquid, and Gas Phases
items.stem:
A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Calculate the molar volume of liquid argon, in cm³/mol.

(b) The molar volume of solid argon at 84 K is 24.7 cm³/mol. Explain, in terms of the arrangement of the particles, why the molar volumes of solid argon and liquid argon are similar.

(c) Explain, in terms of the particles, why the molar volume of argon gas at 273 K and 1.00 atm is roughly 800 times the molar volume of liquid argon.

(d) Describe one difference between the motion of the atoms in solid argon and the motion of the atoms in liquid argon.
items.stimulus:
Argon (molar mass 39.95 g/mol) can exist as a solid, a liquid, or a gas. The table gives the density of argon in each condensed phase at the temperature shown.

Phase | Temperature (K) | Density (g/cm³)
solid | 84 | 1.62
liquid | 87 | 1.40

At 273 K and 1.00 atm, the molar volume of argon gas is 2.24 × 10⁴ cm³/mol.

Answer the following.
items.answer:
(a) Molar volume = molar mass ÷ density = (39.95 g/mol) ÷ (1.40 g/cm³) = 28.5 cm³/mol.

(b) In both solid and liquid argon, the argon atoms are in close contact with their neighbors at all times. Because the atoms are packed nearly as closely in the liquid as in the solid, one mole occupies a similar volume in both phases (24.7 cm³/mol and 28.5 cm³/mol).

(c) In the gas, the argon atoms are in constant motion and are separated by distances that are very large compared with the size of the atoms, so nearly all of the volume of the gas is empty space. In the liquid the atoms touch one another. Therefore the same number of atoms takes up a far larger volume as a gas, about 2.24 × 10⁴ ÷ 28.5 ≈ 790 times the liquid volume.

(d) In solid argon, each atom vibrates about a fixed position and the atoms do not move past one another. In liquid argon, the atoms remain in contact but continually move past one another, so they change positions relative to their neighbors.

criteria.text: Calculates a molar volume of 28.5 cm³/mol for liquid argon.
criteria.evidence: Response divides the molar mass by the density (39.95 g/mol ÷ 1.40 g/cm³) or uses an equivalent conversion and reports 28.5 cm³/mol.
criteria.fix: Molar volume equals molar mass divided by density; check that grams cancel and leave cm³ per mole.

items.title: Balanced and Unbalanced Forces in Three Situations
items.stem:
A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) For Situation 1, calculate the magnitude of the friction force and the magnitude of the normal force that the snow exerts on the sled.

(b) For Situation 2, describe what happens after t = 0 to the east component and to the north component of the puck's velocity. Justify your answer.

(c) For Situation 3, is the bus an inertial reference frame? Justify your answer using Newton's first law.
items.stimulus:
Situation 1: A child pulls a sled across level snow with a rope. The rope is at 37° above the horizontal and the tension in the rope is 50 N. The sled moves east in a straight line at a constant speed of 1.5 m/s. The gravitational force exerted on the sled by Earth is 300 N. The snow exerts a normal force and a horizontal friction force on the sled. Use sin 37° = 0.60 and cos 37° = 0.80.

Situation 2: A hockey puck slides east at 3.0 m/s across frictionless, level ice. Starting at time t = 0, a steady wind exerts a constant horizontal force on the puck directed north. The vertical forces on the puck remain balanced.

Situation 3: A bus on a straight, level road is speeding up while moving east. A small block of ice is placed on the floor of the bus, and friction between the ice and the floor is negligible. A passenger in the bus sees the block slide toward the back of the bus, even though no horizontal force is exerted on the block.
items.answer:
(a) The sled moves at constant velocity, so by Newton's first law the net force on it is zero.
Horizontal: the rope's horizontal component is 50 N × 0.80 = 40 N east, so the friction force has magnitude 40 N (directed west).
Vertical: the rope's vertical component is 50 N × 0.60 = 30 N up. F_N + 30 N − 300 N = 0, so the normal force has magnitude 270 N.

(b) After t = 0 there is still no force on the puck in the east–west direction, so the forces in that direction are balanced and the east component of velocity stays constant at 3.0 m/s. The wind's force makes the net force point north, so the forces are unbalanced in that direction and the north component of velocity changes: it increases from zero, directed north.

(c) No. The net force on the ice block is zero: the vertical forces balance and no horizontal force is exerted on it. Yet an observer in the bus sees the block's velocity change as it starts sliding toward the back. Newton's first law says an object with zero net force keeps a constant velocity, so this observer would not verify the first law. The speeding-up bus is therefore not an inertial reference frame.

criteria.text: Friction force magnitude = 50 N × cos 37° = 50 × 0.80 = 40 N, because the sled's velocity is constant, so the net force is zero and the horizontal forces balance.
criteria.evidence: Response sets the horizontal net force to zero (constant velocity) and finds friction = 40 N from the rope's horizontal component.
criteria.fix: Constant velocity means zero net force; balance the rope's horizontal component, T cos θ, against friction.

criteria.text: Normal force magnitude = 300 N − 50 N × sin 37° = 300 − 30 = 270 N, from balancing the vertical forces.
criteria.evidence: Response sets the vertical net force to zero, including the rope's upward component of 30 N, and finds the normal force = 270 N.
criteria.fix: Include the rope's upward component when balancing vertical forces; the normal force equals 300 N minus T sin θ, not 300 N.

criteria.text: The east component of velocity stays constant at 3.0 m/s, because there is no east–west force on the puck, so the forces are balanced in that direction.
criteria.evidence: Response states the east component remains 3.0 m/s (unchanged) and justifies it with zero net force in the east–west direction.
criteria.fix: Treat each direction separately: if forces along a direction are balanced, the velocity component along that direction stays constant.

criteria.text: The north component of velocity changes, increasing from zero in the northward direction, because the wind's force makes the net force northward, unbalanced in that direction.
criteria.evidence: Response states the north component of velocity changes (grows from zero, directed north) and justifies it with the unbalanced northward force.
criteria.fix: Velocity changes only in the direction of the unbalanced force; identify that direction and state that component changes.

criteria.text: No: in the bus's frame the ice block's velocity changes (it starts moving toward the back) even though the net force on it is zero, so an observer in the bus would not verify Newton's first law, and the bus is not an inertial frame.
criteria.evidence: Response says the bus is not inertial and justifies it by noting the block accelerates relative to the bus while the net force on it is zero, contradicting Newton's first law.
criteria.fix: Test a frame by asking whether objects with zero net force keep constant velocity there; if not, the frame is noninertial.

items.title: Weight and Apparent Weight on a Larger Planet
items.stem:
A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Calculate the gravitational field strength at the surface of Planet P.

(b) Calculate the magnitude of the gravitational force exerted by Planet P on the astronaut when the astronaut stands on its surface.

(c) The astronaut later travels in a spacecraft to a point that is a distance 3R from the center of Planet P, where R is the radius of Planet P. Calculate the magnitude of the gravitational force exerted by Planet P on the astronaut at that point.

(d) Back on the surface of Planet P, the astronaut stands on a scale in an elevator that has an upward acceleration of magnitude 2.0 m/s². Calculate the astronaut's apparent weight.
items.stimulus: Planet P has twice the mass of Earth and twice the radius of Earth. Treat both planets as spheres with symmetrically distributed mass, and ignore their rotation. At Earth's surface the gravitational field strength is 10 N/kg. An astronaut has a mass of 60 kg. Ignore gravitational forces from all objects other than the planet being discussed.
items.answer:
(a) The field strength at a planet's surface is g = GM/R². For Planet P, g_P = G(2M)/(2R)² = (2/4)(GM/R²) = (1/2)(10 N/kg) = 5.0 N/kg.

(b) F_g = m·g_P = (60 kg)(5.0 N/kg) = 300 N.

(c) The gravitational force is inversely proportional to the square of the distance between centers. On the surface the distance is R; at the new point it is 3R, three times larger, so the force is 1/9 as large: F = 300 N/9 ≈ 33 N.

(d) The apparent weight is the magnitude of the normal force exerted by the scale. Taking up as positive, F_N − m·g_P = m·a, so F_N = m(g_P + a) = (60 kg)(5.0 m/s² + 2.0 m/s²) = 420 N. The apparent weight is 420 N, greater than the 300 N gravitational force because the astronaut accelerates upward.

criteria.evidence: Response applies g = GM/r² with doubled mass and doubled radius and obtains 5.0 N/kg (or 5.0 m/s²).
criteria.fix: Write g = GM/r², replace M and r by their multiples, and simplify: doubling r divides g by four.

criteria.evidence: Response multiplies the astronaut's 60 kg mass by the surface field strength of Planet P to obtain 300 N (a consistent follow-through value from the previous part also earns this point).
criteria.fix: Weight is mass times the local field strength; use the field strength for Planet P, not Earth's 10 N/kg.

criteria.text: The distance from the center triples, so F_g falls by a factor of 3² = 9: F = 300 N/9 ≈ 33 N.
criteria.evidence: Response uses the inverse-square dependence on distance from the planet's center (3R, not 2R) and obtains about 33 N (100/3 N).
criteria.fix: Measure r from the planet's center; with F ∝ 1/r², tripling r divides the force by nine.

criteria.text: Apparent weight = normal force: F_N − mg_P = ma, so F_N = m(g_P + a) = 60(5.0 + 2.0) = 420 N.
criteria.evidence: Response identifies apparent weight as the normal (scale) force and obtains 420 N from F_N − mg = ma with upward acceleration.
criteria.fix: Apparent weight is the normal force; apply net force = ma with the acceleration's direction, so F_N exceeds mg when accelerating upward.

items.title: Elastic and Gravitational Potential Energy and the Choice of Zero
items.stem:
A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Calculate the elastic potential energy of the block–spring system when the spring is compressed 0.15 m.

(b) The spring is instead compressed 0.30 m from its equilibrium length. Determine the factor by which the elastic potential energy of the system changes compared with the 0.15 m compression.

(c) Calculate the change in gravitational potential energy of the book–Earth system as the book moves from the shelf to the tabletop, according to Student A and according to Student B.

(d) Explain why the two students assign different values to the gravitational potential energy of the system when the book is on the shelf but agree on the change in potential energy.
items.stimulus:
System 1: A block on a horizontal surface rests against an ideal spring with spring constant 400 N/m. The block is pushed so that the spring is compressed 0.15 m from its equilibrium length, and the block is held at rest.

System 2: A 2.0 kg book and Earth form a system. The book is moved from a shelf 1.50 m above the floor to a tabletop 0.80 m above the floor. Use g = 10 N/kg. Student A chooses the floor as the zero of gravitational potential energy, and Student B chooses the tabletop as the zero.
items.answer:
(a) U_s = (1/2)k(Δx)² = (1/2)(400 N/m)(0.15 m)² = (200)(0.0225) = 4.5 J.

(b) U_s is proportional to (Δx)². Doubling the compression from 0.15 m to 0.30 m multiplies U_s by 2² = 4. Check: (1/2)(400)(0.30)² = 18 J, and 18 J/4.5 J = 4.

(c) Student A (zero at floor): U_shelf = (2.0)(10)(1.50) = 30 J and U_table = (2.0)(10)(0.80) = 16 J, so ΔU_g = 16 J − 30 J = −14 J.
Student B (zero at tabletop): U_shelf = (2.0)(10)(0.70) = 14 J and U_table = 0 J, so ΔU_g = 0 J − 14 J = −14 J.
Both find ΔU_g = −14 J; the potential energy of the system decreases by 14 J.

(d) The position of zero potential energy is a choice made by the observer. Measuring heights from the tabletop instead of the floor lowers every potential energy value by the same amount, mg(0.80 m) = 16 J. The values at a single position differ (30 J versus 14 J at the shelf), but when one value is subtracted from another the shared 16 J cancels, so the change in potential energy is the same for both students.

criteria.evidence: Response substitutes k = 400 N/m and Δx = 0.15 m into U_s = (1/2)k(Δx)² and obtains 4.5 J.
criteria.fix: Square the compression before multiplying: U_s = (1/2)k(Δx)², with Δx measured from the spring's equilibrium length.

criteria.text: The elastic potential energy increases by a factor of 4 (to 18 J), because U_s is proportional to (Δx)² and the compression doubles.
criteria.evidence: Response states a factor of 4 (or computes 18 J ÷ 4.5 J = 4) using the squared dependence on compression.
criteria.fix: Use U_s ∝ (Δx)²: the energy factor is the square of the compression factor, so doubling Δx gives four times.

criteria.text: Both students find ΔU_g = mgΔy = (2.0 kg)(10 N/kg)(0.80 m − 1.50 m) = −14 J (Student A: 16 J − 30 J; Student B: 0 J − 14 J).
criteria.evidence: Response obtains −14 J (a decrease of 14 J) for both Student A and Student B, by direct use of mgΔy or by subtracting each student's values.
criteria.fix: Compute ΔU as final minus initial; with Δy negative here, the potential energy decreases.
variants: a decrease of 14 J for both students

criteria.text: Explains that the location of zero potential energy is a choice made by the observer; changing it shifts every potential energy value by the same constant (here 16 J), so individual values differ but the difference between two positions is unchanged.
criteria.evidence: Response states the zero of potential energy is arbitrary (chosen by the observer) and that this choice adds the same constant to both values, which cancels when finding the change.
criteria.fix: Remember only changes in potential energy are fixed by physics; the zero level is a choice that shifts all values equally.

items.title: Entropy Changes in an Isolated and a Closed System
items.stem:
Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) For System 1, state whether the total entropy of the two blocks increases, decreases, or stays the same as they approach the common temperature. Justify your answer using the second law of thermodynamics.

(b) Explain why the blocks will not spontaneously return to temperatures of 90 °C and 10 °C.

(c) The entropy of the water in System 2 decreases as it freezes. A student says this violates the second law of thermodynamics. Evaluate the student's claim.

(d) For System 1, a second student claims that if the blocks had reached the same final state by a slower process, the entropy of that final state would be different. Evaluate this claim.
items.stimulus:
System 1: Two copper blocks, one at 90 °C and one at 10 °C, are placed in contact inside a closed, perfectly insulated container. The two blocks together form an isolated system, and they eventually reach a common final temperature.

System 2: A tray of liquid water is placed in a freezer, and the water freezes into ice. Energy is transferred between the water and the air in the freezer, but no matter enters or leaves the water.
items.answer:
(a) The total entropy increases. The two blocks form an isolated system, and energy spreads spontaneously from the hot block to the cold block. This process is irreversible. The second law states that the total entropy of an isolated system never decreases and stays constant only when every process is reversible, so the entropy of the blocks increases.

(b) The equal-temperature state is thermodynamic equilibrium, where the entropy of the isolated system is at its maximum. Returning to 90 °C and 10 °C would require the energy to become concentrated again and the total entropy of the isolated system to decrease, which the second law does not allow. So this never happens spontaneously.

(c) The claim is incorrect. The water is a closed system, not an isolated one: energy is transferred out of the water to the air in the freezer. The entropy of a closed system can decrease when energy is transferred out of it. If the water is combined with its surroundings (the freezer and the room it operates in) to form an isolated system, the total entropy of that larger system does not decrease, so the second law is satisfied.

(d) The claim is incorrect. Entropy is a state function, so it depends only on the current state of the system, not on how the system reached it. The same final state of the two blocks has the same entropy whether it was reached quickly or slowly.

criteria.text: States that the total entropy increases, because the blocks form an isolated system undergoing an irreversible process (energy spreading from the hot block to the cold block), and the second law says entropy of an isolated system stays constant only for reversible processes.
criteria.evidence: Response answers 'increases' and justifies it by citing the isolated system, the irreversible (spontaneous) energy transfer or spreading of energy, and the second law.
criteria.fix: Identify the system as isolated, decide whether the process is reversible, then apply the second law's rule for isolated systems.

criteria.text: Explains that returning to 90 °C and 10 °C would decrease the total entropy of the isolated system, which the second law forbids; the equal-temperature equilibrium state has the maximum entropy.
criteria.evidence: Response states that the reverse process would require the isolated system's entropy to decrease (or to leave its maximum-entropy equilibrium state), which cannot happen.
criteria.fix: Ask what the reverse process would do to the isolated system's entropy, and compare that with what the second law allows.

criteria.text: States the claim is incorrect because the water is a closed system, not an isolated one: energy is transferred out of it to its surroundings, so its entropy can decrease.
criteria.evidence: Response rejects the claim and identifies the water as closed (exchanging energy with the freezer air), not isolated.
criteria.fix: Before applying the second law, check whether the system is isolated; a closed system that loses energy can lose entropy.

criteria.text: States that the total entropy of a larger isolated system that includes the water and its surroundings does not decrease, so the second law is satisfied.
criteria.evidence: Response explains that when the surroundings (freezer and room) are included to make an isolated system, the total entropy does not decrease.
criteria.fix: Enlarge the system until it is isolated, then apply the second law to that total entropy.

criteria.text: States the claim is incorrect because entropy is a state function: it depends only on the current state of the system, not on the process used to reach it.
criteria.evidence: Response rejects the claim and explains that entropy depends only on the state (temperature, configuration), not on the path or speed of the process.
criteria.fix: Recall that entropy is a state function; for any claim about a final state, ask whether the final state itself changed.

items.title: Velocity of a Block Under a Time-Varying Net Force
items.stem:
A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Derive an expression for the acceleration a(t) of the block for t ≥ 0.

(b) At what time during the interval 0 ≤ t ≤ 3.0 s is the block's speed greatest? Justify your answer in terms of the net force on the block.

(c) Calculate the block's velocity at t = 2.0 s.
items.stimulus: A 2.0 kg block is at rest on a horizontal, frictionless surface at time t = 0. Starting at t = 0, two horizontal forces are exerted on the block: a constant force of 12 N directed east, and a force of magnitude F₂(t) = 3.0t² directed west, where F₂ is in newtons and t is in seconds. Take east as the positive direction.
items.answer:
(a) Taking east as positive, the net force on the block is F_net = 12 − 3.0t² (in N). By Newton's second law,
a(t) = F_net/m = (12 − 3.0t²)/2.0 = 6.0 − 1.5t², in m/s² (positive is east).

(b) The speed is greatest at t = 2.0 s. The net force is zero when 12 = 3.0t², which gives t = 2.0 s. The block starts from rest, and for 0 < t < 2.0 s the net force is east, so the block moves east and speeds up because the net force is in the direction of its velocity. For 2.0 s < t ≤ 3.0 s the net force is west, opposite the velocity (the velocity is still east, since v(3.0) = 6.0(3.0) − 0.50(3.0)³ = 4.5 m/s), so the block slows down. Therefore its maximum speed occurs at t = 2.0 s.

(c) v(2.0) = v(0) + ∫ from 0 to 2.0 of (6.0 − 1.5t²) dt = 0 + [6.0t − 0.50t³] from 0 to 2.0 = 12 − 4.0 = 8.0 m/s.
The velocity at t = 2.0 s is 8.0 m/s directed east.

criteria.text: Applies Newton's second law with the net force: a(t) = (12 − 3.0t²)/2.0 = 6.0 − 1.5t², in m/s², with positive meaning east.
criteria.evidence: Response writes the net force as 12 − 3.0t² (both forces with signs) and divides by 2.0 kg to obtain a(t) = 6.0 − 1.5t².
criteria.fix: Add all forces with signs to get the net force first, then divide by the mass; never use only one of the forces.

criteria.text: t = 2.0 s: the net force is zero when 12 = 3.0t²; before then the net force is east, along the velocity, so the block speeds up, and after then it is west, opposite the velocity, so the block slows.
criteria.evidence: Response finds t = 2.0 s from the net force (or acceleration) being zero and explains that the block speeds up before that time and slows down after it.
criteria.fix: Speed peaks where the net force changes sign; set the net force to zero and compare its direction with the velocity on each side.

criteria.text: Integrates the acceleration from rest: v(2.0) = 0 + ∫ from 0 to 2.0 of (6.0 − 1.5t²) dt.
criteria.evidence: Response writes a definite integral of its own a(t) from 0 to 2.0 s, or an antiderivative of a(t) with v(0) = 0.
criteria.fix: When acceleration changes with time, integrate a(t) over the time interval; the constant-acceleration equations do not apply.

criteria.evidence: Response obtains 8.0 m/s in the east (positive) direction, consistent with its own a(t).
criteria.fix: Evaluate 6.0t − 0.50t³ at t = 2.0 s, subtract its value at t = 0, and state the direction of the result.
