items.title: Static and Kinetic Friction on a Pushed Crate
items.stem:
A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) The person pushes with P = 15 N, and the crate does not move. Determine the magnitude and direction of the friction force exerted on the crate by the floor, and explain your reasoning.

(b) Calculate the minimum horizontal push needed to start the crate sliding.

(c) After the crate starts sliding, the person keeps pushing with a constant horizontal force of 25 N. Calculate the magnitude of the kinetic friction force on the crate and the magnitude of the crate's acceleration.

(d) The crate is turned onto a different face that has half the contact area with the floor and is pushed so that it slides again. State whether the kinetic friction force on the crate is greater than, less than, or the same as before, and justify your answer.
items.stimulus: A 5.0 kg crate rests on a level floor. The coefficient of static friction between the crate and the floor is 0.50, and the coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.30. Every face of the crate is made of the same material. A person pushes on the crate with a horizontal force P. Use g = 10 m/s².
items.answer:
(a) The friction force is 15 N, directed opposite to the push. The crate is not moving, so static friction acts, and static friction takes whatever value is needed to keep the crate from sliding. With the crate at rest the horizontal forces balance, so the friction force equals the 15 N push. The maximum possible static friction is μₛF_N = (0.50)(50 N) = 25 N, but static friction reaches that value only at the point of slipping; 15 N is less than 25 N, so the crate stays at rest.

(b) On the level floor with a horizontal push, F_N = mg = (5.0 kg)(10 m/s²) = 50 N.
P_min = F_f,s,max = μₛF_N = (0.50)(50 N) = 25 N. Any push larger than this exceeds the maximum static friction, so 25 N is the threshold for starting the crate sliding.

(c) Once the crate slides, kinetic friction acts: F_f,k = μₖF_N = (0.30)(50 N) = 15 N, opposite the crate's motion.
Net force = 25 N − 15 N = 10 N in the direction of the push.
a = F_net/m = (10 N)/(5.0 kg) = 2.0 m/s².

(d) The kinetic friction force stays the same, 15 N. Kinetic friction equals μₖF_N. The coefficient is unchanged because the surfaces are the same materials, and the normal force is still mg = 50 N. Friction does not depend on the area of contact, so halving the area does not change it.

criteria.text: Friction is 15 N directed opposite to the push, because static friction takes whatever value is needed to prevent sliding, and 15 N is less than the maximum μₛF_N = 25 N.
criteria.evidence: Response gives 15 N opposite the push and explains that static friction matches the push instead of automatically equaling μₛF_N = 25 N.
criteria.fix: Treat μₛF_N as only the maximum value; find the actual static friction from the forces it must balance to prevent sliding.

criteria.text: F_N = mg = 50 N, so P_min = F_f,s,max = μₛF_N = (0.50)(50 N) = 25 N.
criteria.evidence: Response finds the normal force of 50 N and multiplies it by 0.50 to obtain 25 N.
criteria.fix: On a level floor with a horizontal push, set the normal force equal to mg; the threshold push equals μₛ times that normal force.

criteria.text: Kinetic friction = μₖF_N = (0.30)(50 N) = 15 N, opposite the crate's motion.
criteria.evidence: Response uses μₖ (not μₛ) with F_N = 50 N to obtain 15 N.
criteria.fix: Once the surfaces slide relative to each other, switch to the kinetic coefficient to compute the friction force.

criteria.evidence: Response computes a net force of 10 N and divides by 5.0 kg to obtain 2.0 m/s², consistent with its own friction value.
criteria.fix: Subtract the friction force from the push to get the net force, then divide by the crate's mass.

criteria.text: The same (15 N): kinetic friction depends only on μₖ and the normal force, which are unchanged, and not on the area of contact.
criteria.evidence: Response states the friction force is unchanged and justifies it with F_f,k = μₖF_N being independent of the contact area.
criteria.fix: Remember that friction does not depend on contact area; check only whether the normal force or the coefficient has changed.

items.title: Kinetic Energy of a Train Passenger in Two Frames
items.stem:
A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) The passenger walks toward the front (east end) of the train. Calculate the passenger's translational kinetic energy as measured by observer T and as measured by observer G.

(b) The passenger turns around and walks toward the back (west end) of the train at 1.50 m/s relative to the train. Determine the passenger's kinetic energy as measured by observer T, and explain whether it differs from your value for observer T in part (a).

(c) For the passenger walking toward the back, calculate the kinetic energy measured by observer G. Then use your results to explain why the two observers can disagree about the passenger's kinetic energy.
items.stimulus: A train moves due east along a straight, level track at a constant speed of 20.0 m/s relative to the ground. A passenger of mass 70.0 kg walks along the aisle at a constant speed of 1.50 m/s relative to the train. Observer T sits on the train, and observer G stands on the ground beside the track. Both observers' frames are inertial.
items.answer:
(a) Observer T measures the passenger's speed as 1.50 m/s:
K_T = ½(70.0 kg)(1.50 m/s)² = 78.8 J.
Observer G measures the passenger's velocity as the train's velocity plus the passenger's velocity relative to the train, both east: 20.0 m/s + 1.50 m/s = 21.5 m/s.
K_G = ½(70.0 kg)(21.5 m/s)² = 1.62 × 10⁴ J.

(b) Observer T still measures K_T = ½(70.0 kg)(1.50 m/s)² = 78.8 J. Kinetic energy is a scalar that depends on the square of the speed, not on the direction of motion, and the walking speed relative to the train is still 1.50 m/s, so the value does not change.

(c) Now the passenger's velocity relative to the ground is 20.0 m/s − 1.50 m/s = 18.5 m/s east.
K_G = ½(70.0 kg)(18.5 m/s)² = 1.20 × 10⁴ J.
The observers disagree because they measure different speeds for the passenger: speed depends on the observer's reference frame, and since K = ½mv², kinetic energy also depends on the frame. Observer T's value is 78.8 J for both walking directions, while observer G's value changes from 1.62 × 10⁴ J to 1.20 × 10⁴ J.

criteria.evidence: Response uses the passenger's speed relative to the train, 1.50 m/s, in K = ½mv² and obtains about 79 J.
criteria.fix: Use the speed measured in the observer's own frame; for observer T, that is the walking speed relative to the train.

criteria.text: Observer G measures a speed of 20.0 + 1.50 = 21.5 m/s, so K_G = ½(70.0 kg)(21.5 m/s)² ≈ 1.62 × 10⁴ J.
criteria.evidence: Response adds the velocities to get 21.5 m/s and computes about 16,200 J.
criteria.fix: Convert to the ground frame first by adding the train's and the walking velocities, then square that speed in ½mv².

criteria.text: K_T is still about 78.8 J, because kinetic energy is a scalar that depends on the square of the speed, not on the direction of the velocity.
criteria.evidence: Response gives the same value as its part (a) answer for observer T and explains that kinetic energy is a scalar that depends only on speed.
criteria.fix: Kinetic energy has no direction; reversing a velocity while keeping the same speed leaves ½mv² unchanged.

criteria.text: Observer G measures 20.0 − 1.50 = 18.5 m/s east, so K_G = ½(70.0 kg)(18.5 m/s)² ≈ 1.20 × 10⁴ J.
criteria.evidence: Response subtracts the walking speed from the train's speed to get 18.5 m/s and computes about 12,000 J.
criteria.fix: When the passenger walks opposite the train's motion, subtract the walking speed from the train's speed before squaring.

criteria.text: Explains that the observers measure different speeds for the passenger because speed depends on the reference frame, so K = ½mv² also depends on the observer's frame.
criteria.evidence: Response attributes the disagreement to the frame dependence of the measured speed, which makes kinetic energy frame dependent.
criteria.fix: Link the disagreement to speed: each frame measures its own speed, and kinetic energy is computed from that frame's speed.

items.title: Evaluating Logarithms and Reading a Logarithmic Scale
items.stem:
No calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Find the exact values of log₄ 64 and log₉ (1/3). For each, state the exponential equation that confirms your answer.

(b) Without a calculator, find the two consecutive integers between which log₂ 20 lies, and the two consecutive integers between which log 0.05 lies. Explain each answer.

(c) On the logarithmic scale described above, find the position of the value 0.001. Point P is at position 1.7 and point Q is at position 4.7. How many times as large as the value at P is the value at Q? Explain.
items.stimulus:
In this question, log v with no base written means the common logarithm, base 10.

A number line is marked with a base-10 logarithmic scale: each positive value v is placed at position log v. For example, the value 100 is placed at position 2, and the value 1 is placed at position 0.
items.answer:
(a) log₄ 64 = 3, because 4³ = 64.
log₉ (1/3) = −1/2, because 9^(1/2) = 3, so 9^(−1/2) = 1/3.

(b) 2⁴ = 16 and 2⁵ = 32. Since 16 < 20 < 32, the exponent that turns 2 into 20 is between 4 and 5, so log₂ 20 lies between 4 and 5.
10^(−2) = 0.01 and 10^(−1) = 0.1. Since 0.01 < 0.05 < 0.1, log 0.05 lies between −2 and −1.

(c) 0.001 = 10^(−3), so the value 0.001 is at position log 0.001 = −3.
Q is 4.7 − 1.7 = 3 units to the right of P. On a base-10 logarithmic scale each unit represents multiplication by 10, so the value at Q is 10³ = 1000 times the value at P. (Equivalently, 10^4.7 / 10^1.7 = 10³ = 1000.)

criteria.text: log₄ 64 = 3, because 4³ = 64.
criteria.evidence: Response gives 3 and the confirming equation 4³ = 64.
criteria.fix: Ask what power of the base gives the argument, and confirm by writing base^answer = argument.

criteria.evidence: Response gives −1/2 and the confirming equation 9^(−1/2) = 1/3 (since the square root of 9 is 3 and the negative exponent gives the reciprocal).
criteria.fix: A square root of the base is exponent 1/2, and a reciprocal is a negative exponent; combine them.

criteria.text: log₂ 20 is between 4 and 5, because 2⁴ = 16 < 20 < 32 = 2⁵.
criteria.evidence: Response names 4 and 5 and brackets 20 between the powers 2⁴ = 16 and 2⁵ = 32.
criteria.fix: List consecutive powers of the base until you pass the argument; the exponents on either side bound the logarithm.

criteria.evidence: Response names −2 and −1 and brackets 0.05 between 0.01 = 10^(−2) and 0.1 = 10^(−1).
criteria.fix: For a value between 0 and 1, write nearby powers of 10 with negative exponents, such as 0.01 and 0.1.

criteria.text: The value 0.001 is at position −3, because 0.001 = 10^(−3).
criteria.evidence: Response gives −3 and writes 0.001 as 10^(−3) (or states log 0.001 = −3).
criteria.fix: Write the value as a power of 10; the exponent is its position on a base-10 logarithmic scale.

criteria.text: The value at Q is 1000 times the value at P, because Q is 3 units to the right of P and each unit on a base-10 logarithmic scale represents multiplication by 10, so the factor is 10³ = 1000.
criteria.evidence: Response gives 1000 and explains it from the 3-unit gap with each unit a factor of 10 (or from 10^4.7/10^1.7 = 10³).
criteria.fix: Find the distance between positions, then raise 10 to that distance; each unit is a factor of 10, not an added amount.

items.title: Amplitude, Midline, Period and Symmetry of Sinusoidal Functions
items.stem:
No calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Find the amplitude of h and the equation of the midline of the graph of h. Show the work that leads to your answers.

(b) Find the period and the frequency of h. Explain how the frequency is related to the period.

(c) Find the values of sin(−a) and cos(−a). Justify each answer using the symmetry of the graphs of y = sin θ and y = cos θ.
items.stimulus:
Let h be a sinusoidal function of x. The graph of h has a maximum value of 14 at x = 3, and the next maximum after x = 3 occurs at x = 11. The minimum value of h is 2.

Separately, let a be a real number such that sin a = 0.6 and cos a = 0.8.
items.answer:
(a) The amplitude is half the difference between the maximum and minimum values: (14 − 2)/2 = 6.
The midline is the average of the maximum and minimum values: (14 + 2)/2 = 8, so the midline is y = 8.

(b) Consecutive maxima occur at x = 3 and x = 11, and the pattern of h repeats from one maximum to the next, so the period is 11 − 3 = 8.
The period and frequency of a sinusoidal function are reciprocals, so the frequency is 1/8: h completes one-eighth of a cycle per unit of x.

(c) The graph of y = sin θ has rotational symmetry about the origin, so sine is an odd function: sin(−a) = −sin a = −0.6.
The graph of y = cos θ has reflective symmetry over the y-axis, so cosine is an even function: cos(−a) = cos a = 0.8.

criteria.text: Amplitude = (14 − 2)/2 = 6, half the difference between the maximum and minimum values.
criteria.evidence: Response computes half of the difference between 14 and 2 to get an amplitude of 6.
criteria.fix: Amplitude is half of (maximum − minimum); do not use the maximum value itself as the amplitude.

criteria.text: Midline y = (14 + 2)/2 = 8, the average of the maximum and minimum values.
criteria.evidence: Response averages 14 and 2 to get the midline y = 8.
criteria.fix: Find the midline as the average of the maximum and minimum values and write it as an equation y = constant.

criteria.text: Period = 11 − 3 = 8, the horizontal distance between consecutive maximum points, where the pattern of h repeats.
criteria.evidence: Response gives a period of 8, computed as the distance between the consecutive maxima at x = 3 and x = 11.
criteria.fix: Measure the period as the horizontal distance from one maximum to the next maximum, not from a maximum to a minimum.

criteria.text: Frequency = 1/8, because the period and frequency of a sinusoidal function are reciprocals.
criteria.evidence: Response gives frequency 1/8 and states that frequency is the reciprocal of the period (one-eighth of a cycle per unit of x).
criteria.fix: Take the reciprocal of the period to get the frequency, the number of cycles completed per unit of input.

criteria.text: sin(−a) = −0.6, because the graph of y = sin θ has rotational symmetry about the origin (sine is odd), so sin(−a) = −sin a.
criteria.evidence: Response gives sin(−a) = −0.6 and cites that sine is an odd function or that its graph is symmetric about the origin.
criteria.fix: Use the odd symmetry of sine, sin(−θ) = −sin θ, which comes from the graph's rotational symmetry about the origin.

criteria.text: cos(−a) = 0.8, because the graph of y = cos θ has reflective symmetry over the y-axis (cosine is even), so cos(−a) = cos a.
criteria.evidence: Response gives cos(−a) = 0.8 and cites that cosine is an even function or that its graph is symmetric over the y-axis.
criteria.fix: Use the even symmetry of cosine, cos(−θ) = cos θ, which comes from the graph's reflection symmetry over the y-axis.

items.title: Testing for a Difference in Household Composting Rates
items.stem:
A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Calculate the combined (pooled) sample proportion and the test statistic. Show your work.

(b) Find the p-value of the test.

(c) Interpret the p-value in context.

(d) What conclusion should the group make at the α = 0.05 significance level? Justify your answer.
items.stimulus:
An environmental group wants to know whether the proportion of households that compost food waste differs between two large towns, Town A (about 30,000 households) and Town B (about 22,000 households). The group selected a random sample of 300 households in Town A and, independently, a random sample of 250 households in Town B. In the samples, 84 of the Town A households and 50 of the Town B households compost food waste.

Let p₁ be the proportion of all Town A households that compost food waste, and let p₂ be the proportion of all Town B households that compost food waste. The group tests H₀: p₁ = p₂ versus Hₐ: p₁ ≠ p₂ at the α = 0.05 significance level. All conditions for inference are met.
items.answer:
(a) p̂₁ = 84/300 = 0.28 and p̂₂ = 50/250 = 0.20.
Combined proportion: p̂c = (84 + 50)/(300 + 250) = 134/550 ≈ 0.244.
Test statistic: z = (0.28 − 0.20)/√(0.2436(1 − 0.2436)(1/300 + 1/250)) = 0.08/√(0.18428 × 0.007333) = 0.08/0.0368 ≈ 2.18.

(b) Because Hₐ is two-sided, p-value = 2P(Z ≥ 2.18) ≈ 2(0.0146) ≈ 0.029.

(c) Assuming the proportion of all households that compost food waste is the same in Town A and Town B, there is about a 0.029 probability of getting a difference in sample proportions of 0.08 or more in either direction (|p̂₁ − p̂₂| ≥ 0.08) by chance in random samples of these sizes.

(d) Because the p-value of about 0.029 is less than α = 0.05, the group should reject H₀. There is convincing statistical evidence that the proportion of all Town A households that compost food waste is different from the proportion of all Town B households that compost food waste.

criteria.evidence: Response adds the successes and the sample sizes across both samples to get 134/550 ≈ 0.244.
criteria.fix: Pool the samples under H₀: add the two success counts, divide by the total of the two sample sizes.

criteria.evidence: Response shows the sample proportions 0.28 and 0.20 and a standard error built from the pooled proportion (about 0.0368), giving z ≈ 2.18.
criteria.fix: In the test statistic's standard error, use the pooled proportion p̂c for both samples, because the test assumes p₁ = p₂.

criteria.text: p-value = 2P(Z ≥ 2.18) ≈ 0.029, using both tails because the alternative hypothesis is two-sided.
criteria.evidence: Response doubles the upper-tail area beyond z ≈ 2.18 (or gives labeled technology output for a two-sided test) and reports about 0.029 to 0.030.
criteria.fix: For Hₐ with ≠, add the areas in both tails beyond ±z; do not report the one-tail area alone.

criteria.text: States that, assuming the proportions of all households that compost food waste are the same in the two towns, the probability of getting a difference in sample proportions of 0.08 or more in either direction (|p̂₁ − p̂₂| ≥ 0.08) is about 0.029.
criteria.evidence: Response includes both the assumption that p₁ = p₂ (in context) and the event of a sample difference at least as extreme as 0.08 in either direction, with the value of the p-value.
criteria.fix: State the assumption (equal proportions in both towns) and the event (a sample difference at least as large as 0.08 in either direction).

criteria.text: Because the p-value ≈ 0.029 is less than α = 0.05, the group rejects H₀; there is convincing statistical evidence that the proportion of all Town A households that compost food waste is different from the proportion of all Town B households that compost food waste.
criteria.evidence: Response compares the p-value with 0.05, rejects H₀, and states a non-definitive conclusion in context in terms of Hₐ (the population proportions differ).
criteria.fix: Compare the p-value with α explicitly, then write the conclusion as convincing evidence for Hₐ, naming both populations, never as proof.

items.title: Simulated p-Value for Mobile Fare Payments
items.stem:
A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Use the simulation results to estimate the p-value of the test. Show how you obtained it.

(b) Interpret the p-value you estimated in context.

(c) What does the p-value suggest about the agency's report that 25% of its riders pay with the app? Explain.

(d) A second analyst took a different random sample of 50 riders and obtained a p-value of 0.41 for the same test. The second analyst concluded that this proves that exactly 25% of all the agency's riders pay with the app. Explain why this conclusion is not justified.
items.stimulus:
A city transit agency reports that 25% of its riders pay their fares with a mobile app. A transportation analyst believes the proportion is greater than 25%. In a random sample of 50 of the agency's riders, 20 paid with the mobile app. The analyst will test H₀: p = 0.25 versus Hₐ: p > 0.25, where p is the proportion of all the agency's riders who pay with the mobile app.

To obtain the null distribution, the analyst used a computer to simulate 200 random samples of 50 riders, assuming p = 0.25, and recorded the number of riders in each simulated sample who paid with the app. The results are shown in the table.

Number who paid with app | Number of simulated samples
6 or fewer | 4
7 | 6
8 | 11
9 | 17
10 | 22
11 | 25
12 | 26
13 | 24
14 | 20
15 | 15
16 | 11
17 | 7
18 | 5
19 | 3
20 | 2
21 or more | 2
Total | 200
items.answer:
(a) The observed value is 20 riders who paid with the app. Because Hₐ is p > 0.25, I count the simulated samples with 20 or more app users: 2 (for 20) + 2 (for 21 or more) = 4. The estimated p-value is 4/200 = 0.02.

(b) Assuming the true proportion of all the agency's riders who pay with the mobile app is 0.25, the probability of getting 20 or more riders who pay with the app in a random sample of 50 riders is about 0.02.

(c) The p-value of about 0.02 is small. If 25% of all riders paid with the app, a sample with 20 or more app users out of 50 would happen only about 2% of the time, so the observed result would be unusual. This provides evidence against the agency's report and for the analyst's belief that the proportion of all the agency's riders who pay with the app is greater than 0.25.

(d) A p-value of 0.41 means that a result like the second sample's would not be unusual if p = 0.25, so the second sample does not provide convincing evidence that the proportion is greater than 0.25. However, a large p-value does not provide evidence that the null hypothesis is true. Other values of p, such as 0.27, could also produce such a sample, so the data cannot prove that exactly 25% of riders pay with the app.

criteria.text: Estimates the p-value as 4/200 = 0.02 by counting the simulated samples with 20 or more riders who paid with the app (2 + 2 = 4).
criteria.evidence: Response counts the simulated samples at or above the observed value of 20 (the direction of Hₐ), gets 4, and divides by 200.
criteria.fix: Count simulated results as extreme as or more extreme than the observed value in the direction of Hₐ, including the observed value itself.

criteria.text: Describes the p-value as the probability of getting 20 or more riders who pay with the app in a random sample of 50 riders (a result as extreme as or more extreme than the one observed).
criteria.evidence: Response states the event as 20 or more of 50 randomly sampled riders paying with the app (or a sample proportion of 0.40 or more), in context.
criteria.fix: Name the event the p-value measures: a sample result at least as extreme as the observed one, in the direction of Hₐ, in context.

criteria.text: States that this probability is calculated assuming that the proportion of all the agency's riders who pay with the app is 0.25.
criteria.evidence: Response includes the condition that the null hypothesis is true, stated in context (if the true proportion of all riders who pay with the app is 0.25).
criteria.fix: End every p-value interpretation with the assumption, for example: assuming the true proportion of all riders who pay with the app is 0.25.

criteria.text: Explains that because the p-value (about 0.02) is small, getting 20 or more app users in a sample of 50 would be unusual if p were 0.25, so the data provide evidence that the proportion of all the agency's riders who pay with the app is greater than 0.25.
criteria.evidence: Response links the small p-value to the observed result being unusual if the null hypothesis were true and states that this is evidence for the alternative (proportion greater than 0.25), in context.
criteria.fix: Translate a small p-value into words: the observed result would rarely happen if H₀ were true, so it is evidence for Hₐ.

criteria.text: Explains that a p-value that is not small means the observed result would not be unusual if p were 0.25, so it fails to provide convincing evidence for Hₐ, but it does not provide evidence that H₀ is true or prove that p = 0.25.
criteria.evidence: Response states that a large p-value only means there is not convincing evidence for the alternative and that it cannot prove, or give evidence for, the null hypothesis being true.
criteria.fix: Remember a large p-value means not enough evidence for Hₐ, never that H₀ is true; other values of p remain plausible.

items.title: Type I and Type II Errors in Apple Shipment Inspection
items.stem:
A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Describe a Type I error and a Type II error in context.

(b) The chain considers a Type II error more serious than a Type I error because bruised apples lead to customer complaints. Should the chain use a significance level of α = 0.01 or α = 0.10? Explain.

(c) With α = 0.05 and a sample of 400 apples, the power of the test is about 0.81 when 8% of the apples in a shipment are bruised. Find the probability of a Type II error for such a shipment. Then, if the chain increased its sample size to 800 apples (keeping α = 0.05), would the probability of a Type II error for such a shipment increase, decrease, or stay the same? Explain.
items.stimulus: A grocery chain buys apples in shipments of 20,000 apples. Before accepting a shipment, the chain inspects a random sample of 400 apples from it. The chain will reject the shipment if the sample gives convincing evidence that more than 5% of the apples in the shipment are bruised. For each shipment, the chain tests H₀: p = 0.05 versus Hₐ: p > 0.05, where p is the proportion of all apples in the shipment that are bruised.
items.answer:
(a) Type I error: the sample leads the chain to conclude that more than 5% of the apples in the shipment are bruised, so it rejects the shipment, when in fact only 5% (not more than 5%) of the apples in the shipment are bruised.
Type II error: the sample does not give convincing evidence that more than 5% of the apples are bruised, so the chain accepts the shipment, when in fact more than 5% of the apples in the shipment are bruised.

(b) The chain should use α = 0.10. A larger significance level makes it easier to reject H₀, which increases the power of the test and decreases the probability of a Type II error (accepting a shipment that has too many bruised apples). The cost is a higher probability of a Type I error, which the chain considers less serious.

(c) P(Type II error) = 1 − power = 1 − 0.81 = 0.19.
With a sample of 800 apples, the probability of a Type II error would decrease. A larger sample size gives a smaller standard error, so the test is more likely to detect that the true proportion (0.08) is greater than 0.05; the power increases and the probability of a Type II error decreases.

criteria.text: Type I error: the chain finds convincing evidence that more than 5% of the apples in the shipment are bruised and rejects the shipment, when in fact the proportion of bruised apples in the shipment is 0.05 (not greater than 0.05).
criteria.evidence: Response describes rejecting the shipment (concluding p > 0.05) when the true proportion of bruised apples in the shipment is actually 0.05, or not more than 0.05.
criteria.fix: Describe a Type I error as: the test finds convincing evidence for Hₐ, but in reality H₀ is true, in context.

criteria.text: Type II error: the chain does not find convincing evidence that more than 5% of the apples are bruised and accepts the shipment, when in fact more than 5% of the apples in the shipment are bruised.
criteria.evidence: Response describes accepting the shipment (not concluding p > 0.05) when the true proportion of bruised apples in the shipment is actually greater than 0.05.
criteria.fix: Describe a Type II error as: the test does not find convincing evidence for Hₐ, but in reality Hₐ is true, in context.

criteria.text: Chooses α = 0.10 because a larger significance level makes it easier to reject H₀, which increases the power and decreases the probability of a Type II error.
criteria.evidence: Response picks α = 0.10 and explains that a larger α lowers the probability of a Type II error (raises the power of the test).
criteria.fix: Remember the trade-off: a larger α increases power and lowers the Type II error probability, at the cost of more Type I errors.

criteria.text: Calculates the probability of a Type II error as 1 − 0.81 = 0.19.
criteria.evidence: Response computes 1 − power = 1 − 0.81 = 0.19.
criteria.fix: Use P(Type II error) = 1 − power, because power is the probability of correctly rejecting a false null hypothesis.

criteria.text: States that the probability of a Type II error would decrease (the power would increase) because a larger sample size decreases the standard error.
criteria.evidence: Response answers decrease and explains it with the larger sample size (smaller standard error, or higher power).
criteria.fix: Recall that larger samples shrink the standard error, so the test detects a real difference more often and Type II errors become less likely.
